paragraphs: R' Yosi HaChorem (a Tanna of a baraita).

He is mentioned in Menachot 36a (supplied לו.; the corresponding saved digital passage is at 37a). He said: We find that the right [hand] is called yad (hand), and Rabbi Natan says: It is not necessary, etc.

And in the Mekhilta, Bo, chapter 7, the statement is repeated, and there [it reads] Abba Yosi and R' Yonatan; Hyman says it should read R' Natan. In the book Sheerit Yaakov it is written (cited in Seder HaDorot, supplied סה״ד) that what we find in Bekhorot 43a (supplied מג.; the corresponding saved digital statement is at 43b), ‘Rabbi Yosi says: Charum means only one who applies kohl to both his eyes,’ is [the statement of] R' Yosi HaChorem, and he was called this after that halakhah.

And Hyman suggests that this may be Rashi’s intent in Menachot 36 (supplied לו; the saved digital gloss is at 37a), where he explains HaChorem as ‘his nose is sunken.’ For Hyman finds it very hard to say that because his nose was sunken they would call him by this derogatory name; rather, he says Rashi’s intent is that this R' Yosi stated the ruling ‘Charum means only one who applies kohl to both his eyes,’ namely, that his nose is sunken.

notes.text: The source prints Menachot36a and Bekhorot43a. Prior supplied context points instead to Menachot37a and Bekhorot43b, but the printed locators are retained here; Hyman’s epithet explanation remains his conjecture.

The supplied Menachot 36a and Bekhorot 43a locators remain beside the corresponding saved Davidson passages at Menachot 37a and Bekhorot 43b, and the Vilna Rashi gloss at Menachot 37a. Four whole selected scalars were read: the first Menachot scalar names Rabbi Yosi HaChorem, the second names Rabbi Natan; the Bekhorot baraita explicitly names Rabbi Yosi. Full Rabbi is supported locally in the Natan report and the Bekhorot quotation; it is not transferred to Hyman’s abbreviated heading, Mekhilta names or later identifications. The Rashi gloss itself uses an abbreviated title. The supplied Mekhilta Bo chapter 7 claim and Hyman’s definite should-read Natan correction remain attributed and independently unchecked. Seder HaDorot is the contextual work expansion of סה״ד; the older tentative Sefer HaDorot note remains historical. Sheerit Yaakov’s identification, as cited by Hyman, and Hyman’s possible Rashi explanation, very-hard-to-say objection and rather conclusion retain their force as arguments, not admitted genealogy or physical description. The Bekhorot passage distinguishes the initial sunken-nose definition from Rabbi Yosi’s both-eyes-at-once formulation; Hyman’s compressed quotations do not state at once, so that primary wording is not added to them. The initial Menachot scalar’s scriptural continuation and the second scalar’s legal argument are likewise not imported into Hyman’s etc. The older bounded nonmatches on Menachot 36a and Bekhorot 43a are not global absence or proof of printing history. All older notes and all three source holds remain unchanged.

The consulted scan of Hyman, volume II, printed p. 740, gives Menachot לז. (37a), and later לז, where the supplied transcription retained here gives לו. and לו. The scan also gives Mekhilta Bo פי״ז (chapter 17), beside supplied פ״ז (chapter 7), while its Bekhorot מג. (43a) remains beside the matching current passage at 43b. In the directly consulted Pischa 17 paragraph, Beeri’s Hebrew has Rabbi Natan and Abba Yoseh Hecharam; Silverstein’s English instead has R. Yonathan and Abba Yossi. These consulted readings explain the transmitted alternatives without proving a particular old printing. Beeri’s embedded note glosses Hecharam as a fisherman; it does not independently establish the person’s identity or Hyman’s explanation of the epithet. The whole Menachot 37a and Bekhorot 43b passages and Rashi’s Menachot gloss remain distinct from Hyman’s proposed reconciliation: the initial sunken-nose definition and Rabbi Yosi’s both-eyes-at-once wording are not silently combined. Hyman’s definite Natan correction, Sheerit Yaakov’s identification as cited through Seder HaDorot, and his possible explanation of Rashi retain their force as attributed arguments; the exact Sheerit Yaakov and Seder HaDorot editions remain uncollated. The earlier notes describe the supplied transcription and the state before this additional inspection.
